title: Lecture 1
overview: This introductory lecture explains what the course is about: understanding computers from the ground up, from transistors and logic up through processors, memory systems, and specialized accelerators. It motivates computer architecture as the field that designs the hardware-software interface to meet goals like performance, energy efficiency, cost, robustness, security, and sustainability. The lecturer also situates the course in current trends such as AI, GPUs, processing-in-memory, heterogeneous chips, and cross-layer co-design.

sections.heading: Course opening: learning, reinforcement, and what this course studies
points: The bell story is used as an analogy for reinforcement learning: repeated pairing of a cue and a reward makes behavior predictable.
The lecturer contrasts reinforcement learning with today’s LLMs, which are built mainly on transformers and neural networks rather than classic reinforcement learning alone.
The course is Digital Design and Computer Architecture, aimed at understanding how computers work from the transistor level upward.
Students will eventually see how transistors form circuits for basic operations such as addition, multiplication, and memory access, and how CPUs, GPUs, and ML hardware are built from them.

sections.heading: Teaching team and research context
points: The instructor briefly introduces his background at ETH Zürich, Carnegie Mellon, Microsoft Research, UT Austin, Michigan, and industry.
He introduces the co-instructor and head TAs, emphasizing that they and the rest of the team are available for questions and lab support.
The research group works on topics such as prefetching, hardware security, homomorphic encryption, and processing-in-memory.
Students are encouraged to ask about research as well as course logistics, because the group’s work connects directly to the course themes.

sections.heading: Why architecture matters: better systems and design metrics
points: The purpose of architecture is to enable fundamentally better computers, not just slightly different ones.
The MIPS R2000 and simple in-order pipelined processors are given as historical examples of designs that once seemed sufficient but were not the end of progress.
Important design metrics include performance, energy, cost, robustness, security, reliability, usability, and sustainability.

For unreliable hardware, a key principle is fail-fast design: detect errors instead of silently returning wrong results; another approach is redundant execution and voting, but that costs extra energy.

sections.heading: Transformation hierarchy and the expanded view of computer architecture
points: Computing is described as transforming problems into algorithms, then into programming languages, system software, the ISA, microarchitecture, digital logic, devices, and finally electrons governed by physics.
The lecturer stresses that humans do not directly “speak the language of electrons,” so the hierarchy is needed to bridge from problems to hardware.
Computer architecture is defined as the science and art of designing computing platforms and the hardware-software interface to meet goals.
The expanded view goes beyond hardware alone: it includes algorithms, software, microarchitecture, and devices, because design choices at one layer affect the others.

sections.heading: What the course aims to teach
points: Students should learn principles and precedents: what existing systems do, why they work, and what trade-offs they embody.
The course includes lectures, readings, homework, labs, and exams; labs will involve implementing and debugging a simple microprocessor.
A major goal is to develop critical thinking and the ability to evaluate design trade-offs rather than memorize isolated facts.
The lecturer repeatedly advises students to focus on long-term understanding and scholarship, not only exam preparation.

sections.heading: Why study architecture now? Top-down and bottom-up innovation
points: Processing-in-memory is used as an example of current co-design trends: putting computation close to or inside memory to improve efficiency and performance.
Architecture matters because it helps adapt to new workloads and technologies and supports applications like AI and VR.
Innovation can happen at the top of the stack through better algorithms and software, or at the bottom through new devices, materials, and circuits; both matter.
Many architectural concepts, such as pipelining, out-of-order execution, and prefetching, are relevant beyond hardware and can also inform software thinking.

sections.heading: Course logistics, resources, and extra credit
points: The course uses Moodle, office hours, the course website, and a large teaching team for support; technical questions should go to Moodle.
Labs require partner selection and FPGA boards are limited, so students cannot work individually.
Readings from the textbooks are assigned mainly for the fundamental first half of the course.
An extra-credit assignment asks students to watch a research talk on RowHammer and reflect on it without using AI tools.

sections.heading: Roadmap of the technical material and processor types
points: The core components of a computer are computation, communication, and storage; the course later connects these to von Neumann-style organization.
The roadmap starts with transistors, then combinational logic, Boolean algebra, sequential logic, HDL design, timing, and verification.
The course then moves to ISA, assembly, microarchitecture, CPUs, GPUs, and memory systems.

A major theme is the difference between general-purpose processors and special-purpose accelerators: general-purpose machines are flexible, while special-purpose ones are faster and more efficient for a narrow task.
Modern SoCs are heterogeneous, containing CPUs, GPUs, neural engines, caches, FPGAs, ASICs, and other accelerators; the labs will build a small microprocessor on an FPGA using Verilog.

takeaways: Computer architecture is about designing whole computing systems and their interfaces, not just isolated hardware blocks.

The course’s core mindset is to ask what can be made fundamentally better and to evaluate designs using multiple metrics, especially performance, energy, cost, robustness, security, and sustainability.
A central organizing idea is the transformation hierarchy from problems and algorithms down to electrons.
General-purpose and special-purpose hardware are a major trade-off: flexibility versus efficiency.
The course will focus heavily on transistors, logic, microarchitecture, ISA, and memory, with labs that build a microprocessor on an FPGA.
Students should prioritize understanding and critical thinking; many lecture concepts are meant to be useful long after the exam.
